URINE__Dipstick & Microscopy:
The urine dipstick is a cheap, near-patient reagent strip that is dunked in fresh urine and read against a colour chart at fixed times. Each pad screens for a different analyte, giving a rapid semi-quantitative snapshot that guides whether a UTI, glomerular disease, diabetes, liver disease or haematuria needs formal confirmatory testing. It is a screening tool, not a diagnosis — every clinically significant result must be interpreted with the history and confirmed by microscopy, culture, protein:creatinine ratio, or blood tests.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

The dipstick is used to screen for urinary tract infection, haematuria, proteinuria, glycosuria and metabolic/hepatic disturbance in acutely unwell patients, antenatal clinics, diabetic reviews and any patient with urinary or systemic symptoms. Each reagent pad carries a chemistry that changes colour in proportion to the analyte concentration.

🩸Blood
Peroxidase-like activity of haem; positive with red cells, free haemoglobin or myoglobin
🧪Protein
Detects albumin only — misses Bence-Jones light chains
⚪Leucocyte esterase
Enzyme from neutrophils → pyuria (inflammation/infection)
🦠Nitrites
Nitrate reduced to nitrite by Gram-negative bacteria (e.g. E. coli)
🍬Glucose
Glycosuria once serum glucose exceeds the renal threshold
🔥Ketones
Acetoacetate/acetone — starvation, DKA, vomiting
🟡Bilirubin / urobilinogen
Hepatobiliary and haemolytic disease markers
⚗️pH / specific gravity
Acid-base clues and urine concentration/hydration
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Use a fresh, ideally midstream, sample tested within a short window of voiding.

Collect fresh urine — delayed testing causes bacterial overgrowth, nitrite loss and pH drift, giving false results.
Fully immerse all pads briefly, then draw the edge along the container rim to remove excess urine and prevent colour run-off between pads.
Hold horizontally and read each pad at its stated time (typically 30–120 seconds) against the manufacturer's colour chart in good light.
Nitrites in particular require urine to have dwelt in the bladder for several hours, so a first-morning sample maximises sensitivity.
3INTERPRETATION
Leucocyte esterase + nitrite BOTH positive→UTI highly likely — treat symptomatic patient, send MSU/culture
Nitrite negative but leucocytes + symptoms→UTI still possible (non-nitrate-reducer / frequent voiding) — do not exclude
Blood positive, no red cells on microscopy→Myoglobinuria or haemoglobinuria — consider rhabdomyolysis/haemolysis
Persistent visible or non-visible haematuria→Investigate for renal/urological malignancy and glomerular disease
Protein positive→Quantify with urine albumin:creatinine or protein:creatinine ratio
Glucose positive (serum glucose > ~10 mmol/L threshold)→Glycosuria — screen for diabetes (or SGLT2 inhibitor / pregnancy / renal glycosuria)
Glucose + ketones both strongly positive→Suspect diabetic ketoacidosis — check capillary/blood ketones and gas urgently
Bilirubin positive with raised urobilinogen→Hepatocellular/obstructive jaundice; isolated high urobilinogen → haemolysis
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Blood pad: false positives from myoglobin and free haemoglobin — always confirm true haematuria with microscopy for red cells.
Protein pad detects albumin and is insensitive to Bence-Jones light chains, giving dipstick-negative proteinuria in myeloma.
Nitrites: false negatives with frequent voiding, dilute urine, low dietary nitrate, and non-nitrate-reducing organisms (Enterococcus, Staphylococcus saprophyticus).
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: a positive dipstick without symptoms should not be treated (except in pregnancy) — overtreatment drives resistance.
Contaminated or stale samples, heavy vaginal discharge, ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and some drugs distort several pads.
🚩 A negative protein pad does NOT exclude significant proteinuria — it misses Bence-Jones protein (free light chains). If myeloma is suspected (bone pain, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment), send serum and urine protein electrophoresis / free light chains regardless of the dipstick. Likewise a negative nitrite does not exclude UTI in a symptomatic patient.
🎓 In an asymptomatic patient, dipstick is only reliable for RULING OUT UTI when BOTH leucocytes and nitrites are negative. When both are positive infection is likely, but a symptomatic patient should be treated on clinical grounds and an MSU sent for culture irrespective of the strip.

Urine microscopy, culture & sensitivity (MC&S) is the laboratory examination of a urine sample to confirm and characterise a urinary tract infection (UTI). It quantifies bacteria (culture), detects white cells and organisms (microscopy), and tests which antibiotics will kill the isolate (sensitivities) — turning a clinical suspicion of UTI into a microbiological diagnosis that guides targeted therapy.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

MC&S is used when a UTI needs microbiological confirmation rather than empirical treatment alone: recurrent, complicated, or pyelonephritic infection, failed first-line therapy, catheterised or pregnant patients, men, children, and suspected sterile pyuria. The principle is that a true infection produces a heavy, pure growth of a single uropathogen with an accompanying inflammatory (pyuric) response, whereas contamination yields scanty or mixed growth.

Simple, non-pregnant women with classic dysuria often do NOT need MC&S — treat empirically; culture is reserved for atypical or treatment-failure cases.
Common uropathogens: Escherichia coli (~75–80%), Klebsiella, Proteus (urease-producing, stone-associated), Enterococcus, Staphylococcus saprophyticus (young women).
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — COLLECTION

A midstream clean-catch specimen (MSU) is standard: the patient cleans the urethral meatus, voids the first portion into the toilet, then collects the middle stream into a sterile container. Discarding the first stream flushes away distal urethral and perineal flora, reducing contamination.

Sample into a boric-acid (red-top) container if transport will be delayed — boric acid preserves the bacterial count; otherwise refrigerate at 4°C and process within 4 hours (delay at room temperature lets contaminants multiply and falsely raise counts).
Alternatives: catheter specimen (CSU) from the sampling port (never the bag), clean-catch/bag urine in infants, or suprapubic aspiration in neonates.
3INTERPRETATION — COUNTS, PYURIA & CONTAMINANTS

Culture quantifies colony-forming units per millilitre (CFU/mL); microscopy counts white cells (pyuria), red cells and epithelial cells and looks for organisms; sensitivities then map the isolate against an antibiotic panel.

≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism (Kass criterion)→Significant bacteriuria — genuine UTI
10³–10⁴ CFU/mL WITH symptoms + pyuria→Clinically significant — treat (lower threshold accepted in symptomatic patients)
Pyuria ≥10 WBC/mm³ (or leucocyte esterase positive)→Inflammatory response supporting infection
Nitrites positive on dipstick→Enterobacteriaceae reducing nitrate → nitrite (specific for coliform UTI)
Squamous epithelial cells / three or more organisms (mixed growth)→Contaminated sample — likely perineal flora, repeat MSU
🧫Pure heavy growth
Single organism ≥10⁵ CFU/mL — true UTI
⚪Pyuria
Raised urinary WBC — inflammation
🔬Epithelial cells
Skin/perineal contamination marker
💊Sensitivities
S/R panel directs targeted antibiotic
4PITFALLS — STERILE PYURIA & ASYMPTOMATIC BACTERIURIA

Sterile pyuria = white cells present but routine culture negative. It flags organisms that do not grow on standard media or a non-infective inflammatory cause.

Pyuria + sterile routine culture→Think TB (send early-morning urines), Chlamydia/gonorrhoea urethritis, recently/partly treated UTI, stones, catheter, interstitial cystitis, tumour
≥10⁵ CFU/mL but NO symptoms→Asymptomatic bacteriuria — do NOT treat except in pregnancy or before urological instrumentation
Sensitivities can lag the clinical need — culture takes ~24–48h, so empirical therapy (e.g. nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim per local guidance) is started and refined once results return.
Catheterised patients are almost always colonised; only sample and treat when systemically unwell, not for cloudy or smelly urine alone.
🚩 Do NOT treat asymptomatic bacteriuria with antibiotics — it drives resistance and offers no benefit — EXCEPT in pregnancy (untreated bacteriuria risks pyelonephritis and preterm birth) or before urological surgery. And never dismiss persistent sterile pyuria: it may be the only clue to renal TB, so send three early-morning urine samples for AFB/mycobacterial culture.
🎓 High-yield: Proteus mirabilis UTI produces urease, splits urea to ammonia, alkalinises the urine (pH >7) and predisposes to struvite (magnesium-ammonium-phosphate) staghorn calculi — a very common exam link. Remember Kass's threshold of ≥10⁵ CFU/mL and that symptomatic patients justify treating at counts as low as 10³–10⁴.

Urinary casts are cylindrical moulds that form within the lumen of renal tubules, taking the shape of the tubule in which they set. Their protein scaffold is Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin), secreted by the thick ascending limb and distal tubule; whatever is trapped in this matrix — red cells, white cells, tubular debris — tells you where in the nephron the pathology lies. Cast identification on phase-contrast microscopy of fresh urine is a cheap, high-yield bedside investigation that localises renal disease to the glomerulus, tubule, interstitium or collecting system.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Examine the urinary sediment whenever acute kidney injury, haematuria, proteinuria or unexplained renal impairment needs localising. Casts form where flow is sluggish and urine is concentrated and acidic, favouring gelation of Tamm-Horsfall protein around any cellular or granular content present in the tubule.

The matrix (Tamm-Horsfall protein) is constant; the inclusions define the cast type and hence the diagnosis.
A cast proves the material was formed within the nephron, not from lower-tract bleeding or contamination — e.g. an RBC cast localises bleeding to the glomerulus.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Collect a fresh mid-stream sample and examine within 1–2 hours (casts lyse on standing). Centrifuge ~10 mL at low speed, decant, resuspend the sediment and examine under low light. Phase-contrast microscopy is preferred; a supravital stain (e.g. Sternheimer-Malbin) aids cellular detail.

Scan the low-power field edges — casts drift to the coverslip margins.
Delay, alkaline urine and dilute urine all dissolve casts, causing false negatives.
3INTERPRETATION

Match the cast to the compartment of the nephron it implicates:

RED CELL cast→Glomerulonephritis / nephritic syndrome — pathognomonic of glomerular bleeding
WHITE CELL cast→Pyelonephritis or acute interstitial nephritis
GRANULAR (“muddy brown”) cast→Acute tubular necrosis (ATN)
WAXY / BROAD cast→Chronic kidney disease / advanced renal failure (dilated atrophic tubules)
HYALINE cast→Normal / benign — dehydration, strenuous exercise, loop diuretics
🩸RBC cast
Glomerulonephritis — dysmorphic RBCs, active sediment
⚪WBC cast
Pyelonephritis / interstitial nephritis
🟤Granular
Muddy-brown → acute tubular necrosis
🕯️Waxy / broad
Chronic / end-stage renal failure
💧Hyaline
Benign — dehydration, exercise
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Hyaline casts are non-specific and may appear in health — do not over-interpret them in isolation.
Absence of casts never excludes renal disease; degradation with delay is common.
Distinguish true casts from pseudo-casts (mucus threads, fibres) — casts have parallel sides and rounded ends.
Interpret sediment alongside eGFR, urine protein:creatinine ratio and clinical context.
🚩 Red cell casts signify active glomerular bleeding and should be treated as a nephrological emergency — they mandate urgent assessment for rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis with early renal function, complement, ANCA/anti-GBM serology and consideration of biopsy, as untreated GN can destroy kidney function within days.
🎓 Three-line exam mantra: RBC cast = glomerulonephritis; muddy-brown granular cast = acute tubular necrosis; WBC cast = pyelonephritis.

Urine cytology is the microscopic examination of exfoliated urothelial cells shed into the urine, stained (classically by the Papanicolaou method) and assessed by a cytopathologist for features of malignancy. It is a non-invasive adjunct in the investigation of haematuria and known/suspected urothelial carcinoma. Its great strength is high specificity for high-grade disease and carcinoma in situ (CIS); its great weakness is poor sensitivity for low-grade papillary tumours, so it complements — but never replaces — cystoscopy.

1Indication & principle

Urothelial (transitional) carcinoma cells are continually shed from the lining of the bladder, ureters and renal pelvis into the urine. Malignant cells lose their normal cohesion and display abnormal nuclear features, which a cytopathologist can detect in the sediment.

Part of the haematuria workup alongside flexible cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging (CT urogram / USS).
Surveillance of known non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, especially high-grade disease or CIS.
Investigation of unexplained persistent irritative lower urinary tract symptoms where CIS is suspected.
🧪High-grade UC
Sheds atypical cells readily → cytology sensitive
🔬CIS
Flat, invisible at cystoscopy → cytology invaluable
📉Low-grade UC
Cohesive, bland cells → frequently missed
2How it is performed

Specimen quality is everything — adequate cellularity and prompt fixation determine the yield.

Voided specimen: a fresh, mid-morning (not first-void) sample is preferred; overnight urine is degenerate and unreliable because of prolonged cellular breakdown.
Bladder-wash / barbotage: saline instilled and aspirated at cystoscopy yields more, better-preserved cells and higher sensitivity than voided urine.
Send promptly or fix appropriately; three specimens on separate days improve yield over a single sample.
First morning void→Avoid — cells degenerate overnight, high false negatives
Bladder wash vs voided→Higher cellular yield & sensitivity
3Interpretation (Paris System)

Modern reporting uses the Paris System, which centres on detecting high-grade urothelial carcinoma. The key malignant feature is a raised nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio with hyperchromatic, irregular nuclei.

Negative for high-grade UC→No malignant cells — does NOT exclude low-grade tumour
Atypical urothelial cells (AUC)→Indeterminate — correlate with cystoscopy, may repeat
Suspicious for high-grade UC→Strong concern — proceed to cystoscopy ± biopsy
Positive for high-grade UC→Diagnostic — high specificity, act on it
N:C ratio ≥ 0.7 + hyperchromasia→Cytological hallmark of high-grade malignancy
4Pitfalls & limitations
Low sensitivity for low-grade tumours (often <30%) — bland cells resemble benign urothelium.
False positives / atypia: stones, indwelling catheters, urinary tract infection, and intravesical BCG or chemotherapy cause reactive atypia mimicking malignancy.
Operator- and observer-dependent; requires an experienced cytopathologist.
🚩 A negative urine cytology does NOT exclude bladder cancer. In visible (macroscopic) haematuria, cystoscopy is mandatory regardless of the cytology result. Cytology is an adjunct — most useful for high-grade disease and CIS — and can never be used alone to rule out malignancy.
🎓 Remember the trade-off: urine cytology is highly specific but poorly sensitive. It excels at catching flat CIS (which is invisible at cystoscopy) and high-grade tumours, but misses low-grade papillary lesions — so a positive result is meaningful while a negative one is reassuring only in combination with cystoscopy.
URINE__Renal Function & Electrolytes:
The urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) quantifies proteinuria on a single random (spot) urine sample by measuring urinary protein against urinary creatinine, correcting for how dilute or concentrated the urine is. It gives a reliable estimate of daily protein excretion without the inaccuracy and inconvenience of a 24-hour collection, and is used to detect and stage glomerular disease, nephrotic syndrome and proteinuric chronic kidney disease.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Ordered when dipstick shows proteinuria, to investigate oedema/suspected nephrotic syndrome, and to quantify and monitor proteinuria in known glomerular or renal disease. The principle: creatinine is excreted at a fairly constant rate across the day, so expressing protein as a ratio to creatinine cancels out variation in urine concentration — a spot sample then approximates 24-hour excretion.

Units are mg/mmol (protein per creatinine).
A PCR of ~100 mg/mmol roughly equates to ~1 g of protein per 24 hours.
Detects all urinary proteins (albumin plus globulins), so it captures overflow proteinuria too.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A single random spot urine sample is sent to the lab; no timed collection is needed. An early-morning (first-void) sample is preferred as it minimises the effect of posture (orthostatic proteinuria) and gives the most reproducible result. The lab measures total protein and creatinine and reports the ratio; no special patient preparation or fasting is required.

Replaces the cumbersome, error-prone 24-hour urine collection.
Convenient for repeated monitoring in clinic.
3INTERPRETATION & CUT-OFFS
PCR <15 mg/mmol→Normal — no significant proteinuria
PCR ≥50 mg/mmol→Clinically significant proteinuria warranting investigation
PCR ≥100 mg/mmol→Approx. ≥1 g/24h — consider nephrology referral
PCR >300–350 mg/mmol→Nephrotic-range proteinuria (>3–3.5 g/24h)
🧪Total protein
Numerator — captures albumin + globulins
⚗️Creatinine
Denominator — corrects for urine concentration
🎯Nephrotic PCR
>300–350 mg/mmol = >3–3.5 g/24h
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Falsely elevated by strenuous exercise, fever, UTI, menstrual contamination and gross haematuria.
Very high or very low muscle mass alters creatinine excretion and skews the ratio.
PCR measures total protein, so it is less sensitive for the low-level albuminuria of early diabetic or CKD screening.
🚩 A PCR in the nephrotic range (>300–350 mg/mmol) with oedema, hypoalbuminaemia and hyperlipidaemia is nephrotic syndrome and needs urgent nephrology referral. For early diabetic nephropathy and CKD screening, use the more sensitive albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR), which detects albuminuria that PCR can miss.
🎓 Remember the conversion: PCR (mg/mmol) ÷ 100 ≈ protein in g/24h, so PCR 300 ≈ 3 g/day. NICE recommends ACR (not PCR) as the first-line test for detecting proteinuria in CKD and diabetes because it is more sensitive at low levels.

The urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) quantifies albumin leak into the urine relative to creatinine, correcting for urine concentration. It is the preferred test for the early detection of kidney disease and the recommended annual screen for diabetic nephropathy, being far more sensitive and specific for the small amounts of albumin that mark early glomerular damage than a urine dipstick or protein:creatinine ratio (PCR).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Albumin is a small, negatively charged plasma protein normally held back by the intact glomerular filtration barrier. Early glomerular injury (especially diabetic and hypertensive nephropathy) causes selective albuminuria long before total protein or GFR change — making albumin the ideal early marker. Measuring albumin against urinary creatinine corrects for hydration/urine concentration, so a single spot sample estimates the 24-hour albumin loss without a timed collection.

Annual screen in all patients with type 1 diabetes (from 5 years) and type 2 diabetes (from diagnosis).
Part of the routine work-up and monitoring of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and hypertension.
Albuminuria is an independent marker of cardiovascular risk, not just renal risk.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A first-pass early-morning urine sample is preferred: overnight recumbency minimises orthostatic and exercise-related albuminuria and gives the most reproducible result. The laboratory measures urinary albumin (mg/L) and creatinine (mmol/L) and reports the ratio in mg/mmol.

Avoid sampling during heavy exercise, fever, menstruation, or urinary tract infection — all transiently raise albumin.
An initial raised ACR should be confirmed on a subsequent early-morning sample before a diagnosis of persistent albuminuria is made.
Result is a spot ratio — no timed or 24-hour collection required.
3INTERPRETATION (KDIGO ACR BANDS)

ACR is categorised into three albuminuria stages (A1–A3), which combine with eGFR (G1–G5) in the KDIGO "heat-map" grid to classify CKD and its prognostic risk.

ACR <3 mg/mmol→A1 — normal to mildly increased (normoalbuminuria)
ACR 3–30 mg/mmol→A2 — moderately increased ("microalbuminuria"); earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy
ACR >30 mg/mmol→A3 — severely increased ("macroalbuminuria"); established nephropathy
ACR ≥70 mg/mmol→Refer to nephrology (unless a known cause being treated)
🟢A1 <3
Normal albumin excretion
🟡A2 3–30
Moderately increased; early nephropathy
🔴A3 >30
Severely increased; overt proteinuria
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Transient false positives: UTI, fever, vigorous exercise, menstruation, decompensated heart failure — always confirm with a repeat sample.
Creatinine dependence: very high or low muscle mass alters urinary creatinine and can skew the ratio.
Non-albumin proteinuria missed: ACR detects albumin only, so overflow proteinuria such as Bence Jones (light chains) in myeloma may be missed — use PCR/electrophoresis if suspected.
🚩 In a person with diabetes, a confirmed ACR ≥3 mg/mmol (moderately increased albuminuria) is an indication to start an ACE inhibitor or ARB — even if blood pressure is normal — to slow progression of nephropathy. Confirm the result is persistent (2 of 3 samples over ~3 months) before labelling and act on it; do not dismiss an isolated raised value but also do not diagnose on a single reading.
🎓 Remember the division of labour: ACR for early detection (sensitive to small amounts of albumin — diabetes/CKD screening), and PCR for quantifying heavy, established proteinuria. An ACR ≥70 warrants nephrology referral, and ACR is the value plotted on the KDIGO grid alongside eGFR.

Urine osmolality measures the concentration of solute in urine and, read alongside serum osmolality, reveals whether the kidney is appropriately concentrating or diluting. It is the pivotal bedside/lab test for working up hyponatraemia, hypernatraemia and polyuria — telling you whether ADH (vasopressin) is being switched on or off appropriately for the patient's plasma tonicity.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

A healthy kidney can vary urine osmolality from ~50 to ~1200 mOsm/kg depending on ADH. ADH release is driven by plasma osmolality (via hypothalamic osmoreceptors) and by volume/baroreceptor stimuli. Comparing urine osm vs serum osm shows whether ADH activity matches the plasma state.

Serum osm can be estimated: 2×Na⁺ + glucose + urea (all mmol/L).
High ADH → concentrated urine (urine osm > serum). Suppressed ADH → dilute urine (urine osm < serum).
Used to assess renal concentrating ability, and the ADH response in hyponatraemia, hypernatraemia and polyuria.
🧪Urine osmolality
Solute concentration of urine (mOsm/kg)
🩸Serum osmolality
Plasma tonicity; drives ADH release
💧Urine Na⁺
Separates SIADH from hypovolaemia
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A paired sample is key: send a random (spot) urine for osmolality with a simultaneous serum osmolality, plus paired urine and serum sodium. Interpret always against the patient's volume status on examination.

Avoid recent diuretics, which invalidate urine Na and osmolality.
Water deprivation test: for chronic polyuria/polydipsia to distinguish diabetes insipidus (DI) from primary polydipsia. Baseline weight, serum and urine osm taken, then fluids withheld under supervision.
Urine osm measured hourly; the test is stopped if >3% body weight is lost or serum osm rises >300 mOsm/kg.
Once maximally deprived, give desmopressin (DDAVP) 2 µg IM and remeasure urine osm to localise the lesion.
3INTERPRETATION

Normal kidneys concentrate urine to >600 mOsm/kg with water restriction and dilute to <100 mOsm/kg with a water load. In hyponatraemia the question is whether ADH is appropriately off (dilute urine) or inappropriately on.

Urine osm > serum osm→Kidney is concentrating (ADH active)
Hyponatraemia + urine osm <100 mOsm/kg→Appropriate ADH suppression: primary polydipsia or beer potomania / low-solute diet
Hyponatraemia + urine osm >100 (often >300)→Inappropriate ADH: SIADH (if euvolaemic) or hypovolaemia (if volume-deplete)
Water deprivation: urine osm >600 mOsm/kg→Normal concentrating ability; excludes DI (primary polydipsia)
Deprivation urine osm low, rises ≥50% after DDAVP→Cranial (central) diabetes insipidus
Deprivation urine osm low, no response to DDAVP→Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
Recent diuretics, glycosuria and high urea (e.g. GI bleed, TPN) raise urine osm independent of ADH and confound interpretation.
Partial DI and primary polydipsia can give intermediate, overlapping urine osm (300–600), making the DDAVP response essential.
Chronic severe polydipsia washes out the medullary concentration gradient, blunting the response and mimicking nephrogenic DI.
🚩 SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion: the patient must be clinically euvolaemic with normal thyroid and adrenal function, urine osmolality inappropriately high (>100 mOsm/kg, typically >300) and urine Na⁺ high (>30 mmol/L). Diagnosing SIADH in a hypovolaemic patient and restricting fluid can be dangerous — exclude hypovolaemia and hypothyroidism/hypocortisolism first.
🎓 In any hyponatraemia, a urine osmolality <100 mOsm/kg means ADH is fully suppressed and points to water excess (primary polydipsia or beer potomania) rather than SIADH — the kidney is doing exactly the right thing.

Urine electrolytes — measuring urinary sodium (UNa), potassium (UK) and chloride (UCl) on a spot sample — give a real-time readout of what the kidney is doing with salt and water. Because the tubule's handling of these ions reflects effective circulating volume, aldosterone activity and acid–base state, a single random urine sample can distinguish prerenal (avid retention) from intrinsic renal failure, localise the source of a metabolic alkalosis, and separate renal from extra-renal potassium loss.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — reading the kidney's intentions

A healthy kidney adjusts urinary electrolyte output to defend homeostasis. When effective circulating volume falls, aldosterone and sympathetic drive make the tubule retain sodium avidly, so urine sodium plummets. When tubular cells are damaged (acute tubular necrosis, ATN) they cannot reabsorb sodium, so it leaks into the urine. The same logic applies to chloride in alkalosis and potassium in hypokalaemia.

Uses spot (random) urine — no 24h collection needed for these interpretive purposes.
Ideally sent before fluids or diuretics alter the picture.
Interpreted alongside serum electrolytes, volume status and acid–base results.
2URINE SODIUM — volume status & AKI

Spot UNa is the workhorse for separating prerenal azotaemia from ATN, and for the hyponatraemia workup.

UNa < 20 mmol/L→Sodium-avid state — prerenal AKI, true hypovolaemia, or reduced effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome)
UNa > 40 mmol/L→Tubule not reabsorbing Na — ATN, salt-wasting, or SIADH (in euvolaemic hyponatraemia)
Hyponatraemia + UNa > 30 + euvolaemia→Supports SIADH (once thyroid/adrenal excluded)
Hyponatraemia + UNa < 20 + hypovolaemia→Extra-renal Na loss (D&V, third-spacing) — give saline

The fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) refines this: <1% suggests prerenal, >2% suggests ATN. FENa is more reliable than UNa alone because it corrects for urine concentration.

3URINE CHLORIDE & POTASSIUM — localising alkalosis & K loss

In a metabolic alkalosis, urine chloride — not sodium — is the discriminator, because bicarbonaturia drags sodium out even when volume is low, making UNa misleading.

UCl < 20 mmol/L (chloride-responsive)→Vomiting/NG suction, prior diuretics, volume depletion — corrects with IV saline
UCl > 20 mmol/L (chloride-resistant)→Mineralocorticoid excess — hyperaldosteronism, Cushing, Bartter/Gitelman — does NOT correct with saline

For hypokalaemia, spot UK shows whether the kidney is the culprit.

UK < 20 mmol/L→Appropriate renal conservation — loss is GI (diarrhoea, laxatives) or poor intake
UK > 20 mmol/L (or TTKG > 4)→Renal potassium wasting — diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, RTA, Mg depletion
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
💊Diuretics
Force natriuresis — falsely high UNa, masking a prerenal state
🧪Bicarbonaturia
In alkalosis UNa stays high despite hypovolaemia — use UCl
🩸CKD / elderly
Impaired concentrating ability blunts Na avidity — FENa less reliable
⏱️Timing
A single spot value reflects that moment only — interpret with the clinical trajectory
🚩 A recent dose of a loop or thiazide diuretic INVALIDATES urine sodium interpretation: it drives sodium into the urine, so a genuinely hypovolaemic, sodium-avid patient can show a high UNa and be misclassified as ATN. Always ask about diuretic use before acting on the result — in that setting FEUrea (<35% suggests prerenal) is a better discriminator than FENa.
🎓 Two-line rule for finals: in AKI, low urine Na = prerenal, high urine Na = ATN; in metabolic alkalosis, ignore urine Na and read urine chloride — <20 is saline-responsive (vomiting/diuretics), >20 is saline-resistant (mineralocorticoid excess).

The fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) is a bedside urinary index that answers one high-yield question in acute kidney injury: is this a pre-renal (hypoperfused but structurally intact) kidney desperately clawing back sodium, or has the tubule been injured (acute tubular necrosis, ATN) and lost that ability? It is calculated from paired urine and plasma sodium and creatinine, and — read alongside urine osmolality, sediment and clinical context — it steers whether the answer is a fluid challenge or supportive management of established tubular injury.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE — why sodium handling tells the story

Used to differentiate the two commonest causes of acute kidney injury (AKI) when the history is ambiguous — hypovolaemia/hypoperfusion versus ischaemic or nephrotoxic ATN.

Pre-renal: perfusion falls → renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and ADH activate → tubules avidly reabsorb sodium and water → urine sodium is low and urine is concentrated.
ATN: the tubular epithelium is damaged → it cannot reabsorb sodium or concentrate urine → sodium spills into the urine and the urine stays dilute (isosthenuric).

The FENa corrects urine sodium for how concentrated the urine is (using creatinine as a marker of water reabsorption), making it far more reliable than a spot urine sodium alone.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED — the calculation & samples

Take simultaneous spot urine and serum samples for sodium and creatinine — no timed collection is needed.

FENa (%)→(urine Na × plasma Cr) ÷ (plasma Na × urine Cr) × 100
Because plasma sodium varies little, the ratio is driven mainly by how much sodium is in the urine relative to creatinine.
The complementary fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea) uses the same formula substituting urea for sodium — valuable when the patient is on diuretics.
FEUrea (%)→(urine urea × plasma Cr) ÷ (plasma urea × urine Cr) × 100
3INTERPRETATION — cut-offs & the supporting picture
FENa < 1%→Pre-renal AKI — sodium-avid kidney; give a fluid challenge
FENa > 2%→Intrinsic AKI / ATN — tubules cannot reclaim sodium
FENa 1–2%→Indeterminate / overlap — interpret with sediment & context
FEUrea < 35% (on diuretics)→Favours pre-renal (urea handling is diuretic-independent)

The supporting laboratory picture reinforces the FENa:

🧪Urine Na
Pre-renal < 20 mmol/L; ATN > 40 mmol/L
💧Urine osm
Pre-renal > 500 mOsm/kg (concentrated); ATN < 350 (isosthenuric)
⚖️Urea:Cr ratio
Pre-renal raised (> 100:1 by units); proportionate in ATN
🔬Sediment
Pre-renal bland/hyaline casts; ATN muddy-brown granular casts
4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS — when FENa lies
Diuretics force sodium into the urine, falsely raising FENa in a pre-renal patient — use FEUrea instead.
Chronic kidney disease has a baseline-elevated FENa from adaptive natriuresis, obscuring an acute pre-renal insult.
Low-FENa ATN" causes — contrast nephropathy, rhabdomyolysis, early sepsis and hepatorenal syndrome — can give FENa < 1% despite intrinsic injury.
Acute glomerulonephritis and vasculitis often show a low FENa because tubular sodium handling is preserved.
🚩 FENa is invalid in a patient on diuretics (loop/thiazide-induced natriuresis raises it artefactually) — switch to FEUrea (< 35% suggests pre-renal). It is also unreliable in CKD, with contrast/pigment nephropathy and in some glomerular disease. Never let a single index override the clinical picture: treating presumed pre-renal AKI with aggressive fluids when the true problem is established ATN or an obstructed kidney risks fluid overload.
🎓 Remember the rule of one and two: FENa < 1% = pre-renal, FENa > 2% = ATN. On diuretics, pivot to FEUrea < 35% = pre-renal, and clinch ATN at the bench with muddy-brown granular casts.
URINE__Metabolic & Specialised:
Bence-Jones protein refers to monoclonal free immunoglobulin light chains (kappa or lambda) that are filtered into the urine. It is a classic finding in multiple myeloma and AL amyloidosis, and its detection is a cornerstone of the myeloma screen. Critically, standard urine dipstick is NEGATIVE for Bence-Jones protein because the dipstick pad detects albumin only — so a normal dipstick never excludes it, and dedicated urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation is required.

1Indication & principle

Plasma cell dyscrasias produce excess monoclonal light chains. Because free light chains are small (~22–44 kDa) they pass the glomerular filter, overwhelm proximal tubular reabsorption and spill into urine as Bence-Jones protein.

Ordered when multiple myeloma, AL amyloidosis or another paraprotein-related disorder is suspected (bone pain, unexplained anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, ROULEAUX / raised ESR).
Especially important in “light-chain only” (Bence-Jones) myeloma, where serum electrophoresis may show no intact paraprotein band and the only clue is urinary light chains.
Forms a triad with serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) and serum free light chain (sFLC) assay in the modern myeloma screen.
2How it is performed

Collect an early-morning or 24-hour urine sample. The specimen is concentrated and run on urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP); any discrete band is then characterised by immunofixation to confirm it is monoclonal and identify kappa vs lambda.

Immunofixation is the confirmatory step — it types the light chain and distinguishes a true monoclonal band from polyclonal overflow.
A 24-hour collection also quantifies urinary light-chain excretion (mg/24h), used for staging and monitoring response.
The historic bedside heat test (protein precipitates at 40–60°C, redissolves on boiling, reappears on cooling) is obsolete and unreliable — electrophoresis/immunofixation is standard.
3Interpretation
Dipstick negative, urine electrophoresis shows monoclonal band→Bence-Jones proteinuria confirmed — investigate for myeloma / AL amyloidosis
Immunofixation: single kappa OR lambda band→Monoclonal (clonal) light chain — supports plasma cell dyscrasia
Serum free light chain ratio (kappa/lambda) outside 0.26–1.65→Abnormal clonal excess — sensitive marker, replaces urine assay in some pathways
Dipstick positive for protein but heavy albuminuria pattern→Suggests glomerular disease, NOT specific for Bence-Jones (albumin, not light chain)
🧪Kappa (κ)
One of two free light-chain types; clonal excess raises κ/λ ratio
🧪Lambda (λ)
The other light-chain type; lambda is more often linked to AL amyloidosis
🦴Multiple myeloma
Classic source of Bence-Jones protein; CRAB features
🫀AL amyloidosis
Light chains deposit as amyloid in kidney, heart, nerves
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Dipstick blind spot: the pad reacts with albumin, so light-chain-only disease gives a falsely reassuring negative dipstick despite heavy proteinuria.
A discrepancy between low dipstick protein and high total urine protein (on a lab quantitative assay) is a red flag for non-albumin (light-chain) proteinuria.
Filtered light chains are directly nephrotoxic — they precipitate with Tamm-Horsfall protein forming tubular casts (cast nephropathy / “myeloma kidney”) causing AKI.
🚩 A standard urine dipstick does NOT detect Bence-Jones protein — it can be completely negative in light-chain myeloma. If myeloma or amyloidosis is suspected, specifically request urine protein electrophoresis / immunofixation (and serum free light chains). Light chains are nephrotoxic: heavy excretion can precipitate cast nephropathy and rapidly progressive AKI, so a rising creatinine in a myeloma patient demands urgent nephrology involvement and correction of dehydration, hypercalcaemia and nephrotoxins.
🎓 Remember the discrepancy pearl: minimal protein on dipstick but grossly raised protein on quantitative lab testing = think Bence-Jones / light-chain proteinuria until proven otherwise. The serum free light chain assay is now the most sensitive screening test and, with SPEP, has largely superseded reliance on urine collection alone.

The urine hCG test is a rapid, qualitative point-of-care immunoassay that detects beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin (β-hCG) — a glycoprotein hormone secreted by placental trophoblast — to confirm or exclude pregnancy. It is one of the most frequently performed bedside tests in medicine and is mandatory in any woman of childbearing age before radiation, teratogenic drugs, or surgery.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

After implantation, syncytiotrophoblast secretes β-hCG, which maintains the corpus luteum and rises exponentially in early pregnancy. Urinary β-hCG becomes detectable roughly 1–2 weeks post-conception (around the time of the missed period). The lateral-flow device uses monoclonal antibodies against the specific β-subunit, avoiding cross-reaction with LH, FSH and TSH which share the common α-subunit.

Confirm suspected pregnancy (amenorrhoea, nausea, pelvic pain, bleeding).
Mandatory screen before X-ray/CT, chemotherapy, or any surgery/anaesthetic in a woman of childbearing potential.
First step in the workup of any woman of reproductive age presenting with abdominal pain or collapse.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A fresh urine sample is applied to the test strip and read at the manufacturer’s stated time (usually 3–5 minutes). A visible control line must appear for the test to be valid; a second test line indicates a positive result.

Use the first morning void where possible — it is the most concentrated and gives the earliest reliable positive.
Modern devices detect from a sensitivity threshold of about 25 IU/L of hCG.
No control line = invalid test, regardless of the test line — repeat with a new device.
3INTERPRETATION
Positive (test + control line)→Pregnancy present — site not confirmed; correlate clinically
Negative + still suspicious/amenorrhoea→Repeat in 48–72 h or send serum β-hCG
Positive + pain and/or PV bleeding→Exclude ectopic pregnancy — urgent assessment
Serum β-hCG rising < 63% over 48 h→Abnormal (suboptimal) rise — suggests ectopic or failing pregnancy
Markedly elevated / ‘snowstorm’ on USS→Molar or multiple pregnancy — refer

Serum β-hCG is quantitative and is used where urine alone is insufficient: dating uncertainty, monitoring of ectopic/pregnancy of unknown location, and surveillance of molar/gestational trophoblastic disease.

4PITFALLS & LIMITATIONS
💧Dilute urine
Excess fluid lowers hCG concentration → false negative
⏱️Tested too early
hCG below threshold before implantation is established → false negative
🪝Hook effect
Very high hCG (molar/multiple) saturates antibodies → false negative; dilute & retest
🧬Persistent hCG
Positive for days–weeks after miscarriage/TOP or with hCG-secreting tumours
🚩 Always exclude pregnancy with a urine hCG before ionising radiation, teratogenic drugs (methotrexate, warfarin, retinoids, chemotherapy) or surgery in any woman of childbearing age. A positive test with abdominal pain and/or PV bleeding is an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise — a urine test confirms pregnancy but never its location.
🎓 A single serum β-hCG cannot distinguish intrauterine from ectopic pregnancy — it is the trend that counts. In a normal early pregnancy β-hCG rises by ≥63% over 48 h; a slow, plateauing or falling level points to an ectopic or non-viable pregnancy. A level far higher than expected for gestation suggests a molar or multiple pregnancy.

Urine pH and the urine anion gap (UAG) are simple bedside/biochemical tools used to work up a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis (NAGMA). The central question they answer is: is the acidosis due to gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss (e.g. diarrhoea, where the kidney appropriately ramps up ammonium excretion) or a renal tubular acidosis (RTA), where the kidney fails to excrete acid? The UAG acts as an indirect surrogate for urinary ammonium (NH₄⁺) excretion.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Use when a patient has a confirmed NAGMA (low HCO₃⁻, normal plasma anion gap, raised Cl⁻) and the cause is not obvious. The kidney defends pH by excreting acid as ammonium (NH₄⁺). Because NH₄⁺ is a positive unmeasured cation, high ammonium excretion pulls extra Cl⁻ into the urine, making the measured anions exceed the measured cations.

Urine anion gap = (Na⁺ + K⁺) − Cl⁻ — measured on a random urine sample.
A negative UAG means lots of unmeasured cation (NH₄⁺) is being excreted → kidney is working, so the cause is extrarenal.
A positive UAG means little NH₄⁺ is being excreted → the kidney is the problem (RTA).
🎓 Aide-memoire: “neg = GI, pos = kidney” — a negative UAG points away from the kidney; think of the negative sign as the kidney “dumping acid” correctly.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
Urine pH: fresh, freshly-voided sample measured with a pH meter (not just a dipstick, which is imprecise at the extremes). A first-morning specimen reflects maximal overnight acidification.
Urine anion gap: send a spot urine for Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻; calculate (Na+K)−Cl.
Interpret alongside serum bicarbonate, chloride, potassium and the plasma anion gap.
🚩 The UAG is invalid when urinary ammonium is paired with an unmeasured anion other than chloride — e.g. ketoacidosis (β-hydroxybutyrate), toluene/glue sniffing (hippurate), or D-lactic acidosis. In these the UAG can look falsely positive despite good NH₄⁺ excretion. It is also unreliable in oliguria (urine Na⁺ < 20 mmol/L).
3INTERPRETATION — UAG & RTA TYPES
UAG negative (typically −20 to −50)→Extrarenal: GI HCO₃⁻ loss (diarrhoea, ileostomy) — appropriate NH₄⁺ excretion
UAG positive (≥ 0, often +20 to +40)→Renal tubular acidosis — impaired NH₄⁺ excretion
Type 1 (distal): urine pH > 5.5, K⁺ low, positive UAG→Failure to secrete H⁺ distally; nephrocalcinosis / renal stones, may cause severe acidosis
Type 2 (proximal): urine pH variable (can be < 5.5), K⁺ low→Proximal HCO₃⁻ wasting; part of Fanconi syndrome (glycosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria)
Type 4: urine pH < 5.5, K⁺ HIGH→Hypoaldosteronism / aldosterone resistance (diabetes, ACEi, NSAIDs) — reduced NH₄⁺ production
🧪Type 1 Distal
Cannot acidify urine (pH > 5.5), hypokalaemic, stones/nephrocalcinosis
🧪Type 2 Proximal
Bicarbonate wasting, hypokalaemic, Fanconi syndrome
🧪Type 4
Hyperkalaemic, hypoaldosteronism/diabetes, acid urine
4PITFALLS & SAFETY
Potassium direction discriminates: Types 1 & 2 are hypokalaemic; Type 4 is hyperkalaemic. This is the fastest bedside split.
A urine pH that cannot be lowered below 5.5 despite systemic acidosis is the hallmark of Type 1.
UTI with urease-producing organisms (e.g. Proteus) alkalinises urine and can mimic a high pH — exclude infection first.
🚩 A positive urine anion gap in a NAGMA is renal tubular acidosis, NOT diarrhoeal/GI bicarbonate loss — do not attribute it to the bowel. Untreated distal (Type 1) RTA drives progressive nephrocalcinosis, stones and bone disease, and severe hypokalaemia can precipitate cardiac arrhythmia.
🎓 In Type 1 (distal) RTA the urine pH stays > 5.5 even when the patient is systemically acidotic — the classic examined finding. Type 2 and Type 4 can both acidify the urine below 5.5.

Stone analysis and the 24-hour urine metabolic screen are the two investigations that answer the question why does this patient form stones? Chemical analysis of a passed or retrieved calculus identifies the stone type, while a 24h urine collection quantifies the metabolic drivers (low volume, hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, hypocitraturia, hyperuricosuria, abnormal pH). Together they convert a one-off painful event into a targeted prevention plan and are indicated in recurrent, bilateral, paediatric, or single-kidney stone formers.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Around 50% of stone formers recur within 5–10 years, so identifying a modifiable cause is high value. Analysis is strongly advised after a first stone in high-risk groups (children, single functioning kidney, nephrocalcinosis, family history) and in all recurrent formers. The principle is simple: the crystal composition points to the underlying chemistry, and the 24h urine shows whether the urine is chronically supersaturated for that salt.

🧪Calcium oxalate
Commonest (~80%), radio-opaque, forms across the pH range
🧪Calcium phosphate
Radio-opaque, alkaline urine; think renal tubular acidosis / hyperparathyroidism
🧪Uric acid
Radiolucent, acidic urine (pH < 5.5), gout / high purine turnover
🧫Struvite
Infection stone, urease-producing organisms, alkaline urine, staghorn
⬡Cystine
Cystinuria, hexagonal crystals, faintly radio-opaque, young recurrent formers
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The stone should be strained from the urine (sieve during colic) or retrieved at surgery and sent dry for infrared spectroscopy / X-ray crystallography — not simply discarded.

The 24h urine is collected into an appropriate acidified container while the patient is on their normal, free diet (not during acute infection or an obstructed/acute stone episode). Timing matters:

Discard the first morning void, then collect every drop for exactly 24 hours, finishing with the next morning's first void.
Send at least one collection (ideally two on separate days) — wait ~4–6 weeks after an acute stone/intervention so results reflect steady state.
Measured: total volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, urate, sodium, creatinine (to verify completeness) and urinary pH; paired serum calcium, urate and bicarbonate help interpretation.
3INTERPRETATION

Match the stone type and the 24h abnormalities to a mechanism and a treatment target. Key thresholds:

24h volume < 1 L (or urine < 2 L/day output)→Low volume — supersaturation; first-line fix is fluids (≥ 2.5 L/day)
Urine calcium > 7.5 mmol/24h (M) / > 6.25 mmol/24h (F)→Hypercalciuria — thiazide ± low sodium diet; check for hyperparathyroidism
Urine citrate low (< ~1.7 mmol/24h)→Hypocitraturia — citrate is protective; give potassium citrate (also raises pH)
Urine oxalate raised (> ~0.5 mmol/24h)→Hyperoxaluria — reduce oxalate intake, maintain dietary calcium, treat gut malabsorption
Urine pH persistently < 5.5→Favours uric acid stone — alkalinise urine to pH 6.5–7 ± allopurinol
Urine pH > 7 with staghorn on imaging→Struvite / infection stone — urease-producing Proteus; needs stone clearance + antibiotics
Hexagonal crystals / positive cyanide-nitroprusside test→Cystinuria — high fluids, urinary alkalinisation, tiopronin in resistant cases
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & PREVENTION

Results are only as good as the collection: an incomplete 24h sample (verified against expected creatinine) makes every value uninterpretable, and collecting during infection or immediately post-procedure gives misleading numbers. A single sample can miss day-to-day variation, so two collections are preferred.

General measures for all: fluid to keep urine > 2.5 L/day, moderate sodium and animal protein, do NOT restrict dietary calcium (low calcium paradoxically raises oxalate absorption).
Targeted therapy: thiazide for idiopathic hypercalciuria, potassium citrate for hypocitraturia/uric acid, allopurinol for hyperuricosuria, alkalinisation for uric acid and cystine.
🚩 A struvite staghorn calculus is an infected stone and must be COMPLETELY removed — any residual fragment acts as a nidus for persistent infection, stone regrowth and recurrent urosepsis. Separately, uric acid stones are RADIOLUCENT and are missed on a plain KUB film, so a normal X-ray does not exclude a stone — use CT KUB.
🎓 Citrate is the body's natural stone inhibitor: it chelates calcium and inhibits crystal aggregation. A LOW urinary citrate is therefore a risk factor (not a protective finding), and it is classically low in distal renal tubular acidosis — think RTA in a patient with calcium phosphate stones, alkaline urine and a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.
